--- Meeting header ---
Date: 2027-05-12
Start time (UTC): 2027-05-12T15:00:00Z
Duration (minutes): 42
Meeting ID: ff-20270512-kepler-01
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Flynn (Kepler - Head of Platform), Sofia Rivera (Kepler - Cloud Security), Tomoko Saito (Kepler - NetEng)
Recording: auto-transcription (medium quality) — occasional mis-transcribes
Shared artifacts: Kepler intake deck (link), Redwood security brief (link)
Notes: conversation focused on private/VPC connectivity, region constraints (EU data residency), peering vs PrivateLink, egress controls and pilot plan.

Summary:
Kepler is evaluating Redwood's private deployment option. Primary constraints: EU region data residency for a subset of workloads, strict egress rules (only specific IP ranges allowed), need for audit logs and customer-managed KMS. They prefer VPC peering or a private endpoint (AWS PrivateLink / PSC) rather than internet egress. Timeline: pilot in ~2 weeks if docs/diagram provided. Technical owners: Marcus (platform), Tomoko (network), Sofia (security).

Topics:
- Private deployment options (VPC peering, PrivateLink, Transit Gateway)
- Region & data residency requirements (EU + us-west fallback)
- Egress / NAT & allowed IP ranges
- KMS/HSM and encryption in transit at rest
- Audit logs, retention, SOC2/ISO
- Pilot topology and handoff

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, our se—, uh, Redwood AE. With me is Priya Nair, she's our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Marcus Flynn: Morning, thanks. Marcus here. We're excited to dig in, we've been looking at your private deployment options.
[00:12] Sofia Rivera: Hi all, Sofia from security. Quick heads up — we need SOC2 details and KMS integration info up front.
[00:17] Priya Nair: Yep good point. We'll walk through the networking options and I can show where KMS and audit logging will live in the private offering.
[00:25] Tomoko Saito: Tomoko here — I'm NetEng. Primary concern is that our EU prod cannot leave eu-central-1. We also have an onprem site that uses site-to-site VPN for control plane access.
[00:35] Alex Chen: Understood. For private we support a VPC onramp with either classic VPC peering, Transit Gateway, or PrivateLink / Private Endpoints depending on the cloud. We can also do an on-prem VPN to bridge into the Redwood private dataplane.
[00:47] Marcus Flynn: For latency and security we'd prefer peering if possible. But we also want to avoid transitive egress through public IPs. Is there a recommended pattern for restricting egress?
[00:56] Priya Nair: Yes. Typically we recommend either Transit Gateway with route tables that block 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet, or use PrivateLink so traffic never traverses public IPs. For egress to external services we can pin to NAT in a controlled subnet or use an egress proxy in your VPC. We also support prefix lists for allowed IP ranges.
[01:20] Sofia Rivera: Do you have a customer-managed KMS option? We need keys retained within our AWS account.
[01:25] Priya Nair: We do. In private deployments you can bring your own KMS keys — we support AWS KMS via cross-account policies and also HSM integrations on-prem for air-gapped customers. There are a few IAM steps for granting decrypt/encrypt permissions.
[01:40] Tomoko Saito: Are audit logs accessible in our Splunk/ELK? We need to ingest request-level logs and token usage metrics for compliance.
[01:46] Alex Chen: Yes, logs can be exported to your cloud logging or to an S3 bucket with lifecycle policies. Audit events include request metadata, model variant IDs, redaction status. Might be a slight delay depending on retention and export batch sizes.
[02:00] Marcus Flynn: Ok, timeline — if we get the security brief and a network diagram from you, we can set a pilot within two weeks. We'll need a sandbox in eu-central-1 and a potential fallback in eu-west-1 for DR.
[02:12] Priya Nair: Sounds reasonable. We'll include a sample peering diagram and a Transit GW topology. Also note that cross-region peering has bandwidth and egress cost implications.
[02:25] Sofia Rivera: Cost is one thing, but the bigger is data residency and contractual commitments. Do you support contractual clauses around data residency and deletion?
[02:33] Alex Chen: For private we can add contractual SSO, data residency and data deletion SLAs — we'll work with legal on the specifics. We have enterprise templates but need to review exact language.
[02:45] Marcus Flynn: One technical nuance: our on-prem control plane uses IPSec and we may want to peer that into Redwood's private control plane. Any gotchas there?
[02:53] Priya Nair: It's doable. We typically set up a VPN tunnel from your on-prem firewall to a customer-managed transit or a managed endpoint. We do recommend MTU and rekey timing checks; sometimes the KV cache — kv cache — gets misaligned if packets fragment badly, this was a weird bug we've seen in older setups.
[03:20] Tomoko Saito: (laughs) 'kv cash' in the notes — ok. Regarding DNS, do you support private hosted zones and conditional forwarding?
[03:28] Priya Nair: Yes. We recommend using private hosted zones in your account, and we can configure conditional forwarding so hostnames resolve to private endpoints. There's a small step to add a record that points to the Redwood private endpoint.
[03:45] Marcus Flynn: On the topic of endpoints, on AWS would you prefer classic VPC peering or PrivateLink? We have multiple accounts and want to avoid exploding peering relationships.
[03:55] Priya Nair: For many-account organizations we recommend PrivateLink or Transit Gateway. PrivateLink gives you per-service endpoints with simpler security posture, whereas Transit Gateway can simplify routing for many VPCs but has capacity/attachment cost tradeoffs. If you have dozens of accounts, Transit GW + TGW attachments may actually be cheaper for data transfer inside a region.
[04:20] Sofia Rivera: Our security team will want SAML/SSO and RBAC mapped to Okta. Is that supported on private?
[04:27] Alex Chen: Absolutely, we integrate with SAML IdPs — Okta, Azure AD. We also support granular RBAC roles and attribute mapping so you can federate groups to roles.
[04:36] Marcus Flynn: What about disaster recovery — if eu-central-1 has an outage, can we failover to another region without violating residency for certain customer segments?
[04:44] Priya Nair: We can do per-workload region pinning. For EU-only data, we can keep primary in eu-central-1 and have read-only replicas in another EU region. For full failover we can set contractual limits and maybe geo-fence models/datasets to specific regions.
[05:05] Tomoko Saito: Any hard limits on throughput or concurrent requests in private? We have high QPS inference for in-house search.
[05:12] Priya Nair: Throughput is based on the Dedicated capacity you reserve for private. We can size GPU pools and autoscale based on traffic patterns. For very high QPS we recommend batching and dedicated pools — we'll include model throughput numbers in the follow-up.
[05:32] Marcus Flynn: Ok, let's talk about pilot composition. We want a small sandbox, subset of models, and a defined SLA for latency. How do you validate latency in private?
[05:40] Alex Chen: We run benchmark harnesses in your VPC topology, and we provide token-level latency traces. We can also run end-to-end tests from your onprem to the private endpoint to validate round-trip times.
[05:50] Sofia Rivera: Is there any footprint on our side for the control plane? You mentioned a private control plane earlier.
[05:56] Priya Nair: For private we deploy a lightweight control plane in your account — usually a small-managed service and some IAM roles. The heavy-lift inference nodes run in Redwood-managed tenancy but within peered/private networks. For fully on-prem we offer an appliance option too.
[06:20] Marcus Flynn: That helps. For the pilot, we'll need a checklist: subnet ranges, security groups, list of allowed egress IPs, and contact points.
[06:28] Alex Chen: We'll send an intake checklist. I'll also attach a draft peering diagram and sample security policy. We'll flag any special steps for Okta SAML and KMS cross-account.
[06:36] Tomoko Saito: One more: do you support VPC endpoint policies for filtering what services can be called over the endpoint?
[06:42] Priya Nair: Yes, we can recommend endpoint policies. On PrivateLink you can enforce principal/service level controls. We'll provide sample IAM and endpoint policy snippets.
[07:00] Marcus Flynn: Are there known vendor lock-in issues if we go private with Redwood? Like, can we export models, or move workloads elsewhere later?
[07:08] Alex Chen: You can pin model versions and export logs; models are open-models or customer-supplied weights. We don't require data model lock-in — we support standard ONNX or torch artifacts for portability. We'll clarify export processes in the follow-up.
[07:30] Sofia Rivera: What's the pricing model for private? Is it committed reserved capacity?
[07:36] Alex Chen: Private is a mix — platform fee plus committed dedicated capacity (monthly). We can add burst and overage terms. For pilots we do short-term reserved test tiers.
[07:48] Marcus Flynn: Competitors — we've also looked at Anthropic and Vertex managed endpoints. Your differentiation for us is the production-grade runtime and the private deployment options.
[07:57] Priya Nair: Exactly — our telemetry, rollout policies, and cost controls are key. Also the ability to run identical APIs across hosted and private.
[08:10] Tomoko Saito: On the networking side, we need to confirm MTU, encryption ciphers, and any IPSec parameters your side requires.
[08:18] Priya Nair: We'll include recommended IPSec settings in the checklist and a sample proposal for rekey intervals and cipher suites.
[08:30] Alex Chen: Ok, recap and next steps.
[08:33] Alex Chen: Action items: Priya will draft the pilot topology and Transit GW/PrivateLink pros/cons; I'll send SOC2 + security brief; Marcus will provide region constraints and VPC IDs; Sofia will provide a list of allowed egress IPs.
[08:47] Marcus Flynn: Sounds good. Can we get those docs by EOD Friday?
[08:50] Alex Chen: We'll aim for Friday EOD. If not, Monday morning at latest.
[08:55] Sofia Rivera: We also want a quick security-only follow-up — 30 minutes next week just to go through the SOC2 and KMS details.
[09:00] Alex Chen: Great — I'll schedule a 30-minute security sync for next Tuesday. Priya, any other items?
[09:05] Priya Nair: I'll prepare the network diagrams and sample IAM snippets. Also I'll add sample perf numbers from eu-central-1 nodes.
[09:15] Tomoko Saito: Thanks everyone — appreciate the clarity. We'll review and get the VPC info over.
[09:19] Alex Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the packet and schedule the next calls.

--- End transcript ---
